chunks: From him, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Indeed, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sayyabah has a debt upon a man who has died, and we spoke to him about forgiving it, but he refused.' He said: 'Woe to him! Does he not know that for every dirham, he will have ten dirhams if he forgives it? And if he does not forgive it, then he will have only the equivalent of a dirham, a dirham.'

key_terms.بَدَلُ دِرْهَمٍ دِرْهَمٌ: the equivalent of a dirham, a dirham (principal only)
key_terms.وَيْحَهُ: woe to him / alas for him
key_terms.يُحَلِّلَهُ: he forgives it / releases the debtor

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for forgiving a debt owed by a deceased person in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the spiritual economics of debt forgiveness, emphasizing that releasing a claim against a deceased debtor yields a multiplied reward of tenfold for each dirham. This hadith highlights the virtue of *tahsil al-husn* (seeking the best outcome) in financial dealings, contrasting the spiritual gain of forgiveness with the mere recovery of principal if the creditor insists on payment. It underscores the Shia scholarly view that debt is not merely a legal contract but a trust with significant eschatological implications.
